llama-modchip is a set of ggml/llama.cpp kernel patches, quantization transcoders, and runtime tools designed to run sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) checkpoints entirely in system RAM on x86_64 (AVX-512 / AVX2) and ARM64 (NEON / SVE / Apple Metal) processors:

Fitting 284B DeepSeek-V4-Flash into 64 GB Physical RAM (56.56 GiB on disk, 1.71 bpw): Standard UD-IQ1_S builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284.33B total, 13.17B active across 43 MLA layers and 256 routed experts) occupy 76.87 GiB (82.5 GB), exceeding the ~62.5 GiB of usable RAM on a 64 GB Linux system and causing page-cache thrashing or OOM kills. llama-modchip reduces the checkpoint to 56.56 GiB (60.73 GB) so the entire model plus a 256K KV cache (57.61–58.9 GiB VmRSS) locks into RAM with zero swap. By default, all 6 routed experts per layer (Top-6) are evaluated without pruning. CPU Cache & SIMD Kernel Patches (+77% prefill, +53% decode): Replaces single-column quantized matrix-vector loops during prompt prefill with a 4-level register (ZMM AVX-512BW) + L1D (32 KB) + L2 (1 MB) + L3 (64 MB) multi-column ({8,4,3,2}) tiling schedule (25.0 -> 44.36 tok/s on 16-core Zen 5), register-stationary MQA8 FlashAttention, and non-temporal _MM_HINT_NTA MoE streaming so cold expert weights do not evict hot KV cache lines from L3. Self-Speculative Drafting & Instant Agent Context Restore: Pairs a 1.64 MB L2/L3 Zobrist n-gram drafter (Stockfish-PVS v2) with /dev/shm KV slot snapshots (13.1–32.6 ms restore time for 40-tool Claude Code prompts) and an $O(1)$speculative rollback fix fordeepseek4 recurrent/MLA states.

item.title: Writing as a thinking tool
item.description:
Writing as a thinking tool

In middle school I could not get through long passages no matter how hard I tried. I would read an entire page and find that nothing had registered, so I started taking notes out of desperation. This was the late 80s, and Tony Buzan's mind maps had just reached Turkey. This led me to produce pages and pages of notes that looked like spiderwebs. Creating those notes have helped me tremendously. I made sense of what I was reading by figuring out which branch they would hang off in my mind maps. I realized my pages were not for storing the information as much as they were for processing it.

It took me another ten years to understand why this works so well. During a stretch of PhD procrastination, I read Manuel Blum's advice to graduate students:

You are all computer scientists.

You know what FINITE AUTOMATA can do.

You know what TURING MACHINES can do.

For example, Finite Automata can add but not multiply.

Turing Machines can compute any computable function.

Turing machines are incredibly more powerful than Finite Automata.

Yet the only difference between a FA and a TM is that

the TM, unlike the FA, has paper and pencil.

Think about it.

It tells you something about the power of writing.

Without writing, you are reduced to a finite automaton.

With writing you have the extraordinary power of a Turing machine.

This is a crisp technical claim about which problems you can solve with writing. If you take the paper away, you downgrade yourself by an entire complexity class!

I think this explains a lot about human history as well. Language let us externalize some of our thinking, and our species got smarter. Writing let us externalize even more of it, and we got smarter again. I suspect this is also why LLMs are as capable as they are: so much of our intelligence is already deposited in language that a model trained on it inherits a good deal of intelligence for free.

Out-of-core execution

When we write, we are externalizing our thinking onto paper, and that is what raises our capability to think bigger thoughts. I liken this to out-of-core execution, or external memory algorithms.

A good example of this for me is reviewing a paper. When I read a paper, I think I understand it, and then I sit down to write the review and find out I understood maybe 60% of it. While writing the review, I end up contextualizing the paper better, and get to understand it fully. And sometimes I even realize the ideas are bigger than the authors noticed, and they connect to many other things.

Sometimes the unearthing goes further than understanding one paper. In 2018, I wrote a quick post about the anatomical similarities between Paxos and Nakamoto consensus. I had not started with that thesis originally. I started writing, and the connections got clearer as I went, and that post became the seed for one of our research papers. This is not uncommon, this is called freewriting. This is what happens when you give the machine a tape.

Writing is also the reason I remember anything. I refer back to my own blog constantly. Because I strained my brain writing those posts, rereading them re-fires the same neurons, and I reconstruct the understanding quickly. In this sense, the blog became my external memory. The thoughts I never wrote down do not stick well, because they were never fully thought.

If you think without writing, you only think you're thinking.

-- Leslie Lamport

 Writing in the age of LLMs

Is writing for thinking getting obsolete now since you can now argue anything with a model that has read everything?

Well, the model has read everything except what is in your brain! It knows the literature, the standard framing, and the consensus. But it does not know your half-formed intuition about why the standard framing may be wrong for this particular case. AI made a lot of progress, but I don't trust an LLM to take the creative leap and make a new connection. I think that would require another AI breakthrough. So, if you open the chat immediately on anything, you lose the opportunity to write/think for yourself.

This is a real problem, and it seems to be spreading quickly. We have been celebrating Amazon's six-pager as a great example of writing-for-thinking. Bezos had said: "There is no way to write a six-page, narratively structured memo and not have clear thinking." Unfortunately, with LLMs, that sentence has stopped being true. You can now produce six pages with no thinking at all, and the six pages still look like evidence that the thinking happened.

A model optimizing next-token probability cannot do your thinking. If you trust it to hold the pen, no thinking would get done. As everyone turns their thinking down and becomes a meat-proxy for generated text, if you still keep writing yourself, you would still be thinking for yourself. So writing is now a comparative advantage, and a widening one!

Anyways, enough about why you should write. Here is my advice on how you should write.

Rule 1: Mess up

The first rule of writing club is to produce in bulk with no restraints at all. Don't criticize, don't fix the typos, don't write in full sentences if you don't feel like it. The goal in this phase is to just accumulate text and get to a zeroth draft you can work with.

McPhee argues best for why getting anything down matters so much. Even if you had a bad writing session, it gave your mind something to work with. After you get something down, you can spot problems with it and think of better ways of phrasing things. But none of that happens without the drafted version to react against.

This is also how research papers get written. Open a notes.org file and treat it as a lab notebook: write while you do the work, explore every tangent, produce without any pressure to be presentable. In the Köroğlu post I compared this to the foal fattened in a pitch-black stable before any training begins. The key part of that frame is the stable. During this phase you guard the idea from critics, including and especially yourself. Ideas start out fragile and easily squished. So suppress judgment for a while and see what the thing becomes.

Rule 2: Tidy up

Now you must become the critic, the editor. Forget that you wrote this. Imagine some other guy wrote it, and do a harsh review. Cut ruthlessly. Take delight in deleting text the way you would in deleting code. If you cannot bear to delete a good sentence, move it to a junk buffer at the bottom of the file so you can tell yourself you might bring it back. Spoiler: you won't.

Don't be discouraged by how bad the first draft was. McPhee says the way to do a piece of writing is three or four times over, never once. This is good news. Thinking in multiple drafts takes the pressure off: you don't have to be spontaneous, brilliant on the first pass, or finished today.

I think the reason writing works so well for thinking is that it slows you down while keeping you on the problem. In that extra time, the insights and connections get room to surface. Chunking/abstracting happens in the background. Editing is then the magic trick where you pretend you had an organized thought all along. It is the packaging of the product.

Rule 3: Keep it simple, plain, and succinct

I am an Elements of Style guy. Strunk and White got it right, and their writing still reads fresh decades later. I adore Vonnegut too. His writing is simple as fuck and completely eloquent. It took a lot of balls to write that plainly. Complexity in prose is usually a place to hide sloppy thinking, or a way to weasel out of taking a stance. If you can't say it plainly, you probably haven't thought it through yet. And the way you think it through is by writing/editing.

Rule 4: Write without expectations

Write for yourself. The audience I have in mind is me. If others read it, that is a bonus, but the motivation has to be intrinsic, because the external rewards are far too delayed and too random to steer on. Writing like no one is watching also frees you up, and you can decide afterwards how much to share. Get your dopamine hit from the writing itself, not from people reading or sharing what you wrote, as that is very unreliable.

I have been writing and sharing on this blog since 2011, and around 2016 I started running into people at conferences who read it. I assumed it was a fluke, but it kept happening. Writing with a human voice turns out to get a lot of attention, and I am still surprised by how much. Paradoxically, you seem to get an audience only if you weren't doing it for the audience.

Rule 5: Put it on the schedule

You should stop trying to get inspiration to write and start scheduling it. Waiting for inspiration doesn't work, instead, putting your butt on seat and writing breeds good ideas for writing.

I find that keeping a posting schedule for the blog keeps me in "a writing frame of mind", which is really "a noticing frame of mind". Many weeks I tell myself a topic isn't interesting, but I start writing about it anyway, and then, what do you know, I am startled by the fount of interesting things that surfaces.

I also feel relieved after writing something as the thought is out of my system, I have closure on it, and I have room to think new thoughts. If a week goes by without a post, I feel clogged. So put writing on the calendar and keep it there until it no longer needs to be on the calendar.

item.title: I'm not a fan of Deno's security model (2024)
item.description:
Iâm not a fan of Denoâs security model

this has been bothering me for a while now, so I want to write down my thoughts so I can get it out of my head and move on. weâre gonna talk about how Deno approaches security, specifically with its permissions system, and why I think this approach is fundamentally insecure and misleading.

wait, whatâs Deno?

Deno is a language runtime for JavaScript. it consists of a standard library, a package manager, a TypeScript transpiler and a bunch of other stuff thatâs not important for our story. itâs not a JavaScript implementation, so it does not interpret or compile JavaScript, it reuses V8 for that.

one of the flagship features of Deno is its permission system (itâs under the âSecure by defaultâ header on their landing page). the idea is simple: as JS code running in Deno needs the standard library to access the outside world, Deno can choose which accesses it allows or disallows, so when you run

shell deno run --allow-read=/tmp/dir --allow-run=uname code.ts

the standard library will only allow code.ts to read /tmp/dir and run uname.

additionally, a program can request permissions at runtime, so code like

typescript const r = { name: "read", path: "/tmp/dir" } as const; await Deno.permissions.request(r);

will display a nice little prompt in the terminal:

â â ï¸ Deno requests read access to "/tmp/dir". â Requested by `Deno.permissions.request()` API. â Run again with --allow-read to bypass this prompt. â Allow? [y/n/A] (y = yes, allow; n = no, deny; A = allow all read permissions) >

and you can grant or refuse it.

(aside: I really miss this feature in browser extensions. currently, if your extension needs potential access to any website, it needs to request actual access to all the websites, which is less than ideal)

if you like puzzles, this is the point where you can stop and think about what could go wrong with this system.

the prompts problem

of the two specific issues I want to point out this is the less severe one. weâll discuss it first because this was the first thing I noticed and it kinda immediately irked me when I first read about this.

(if youâre only interested in the more juicy part, you can skip to the next section).

so, this nice little prompt is displayed in the terminal. itâs not, like, a PolKit GUI window or anything, itâs just text on stdout waiting for input from stdin. this is a wild thing to do.

you see, terminal has a somewhat weird API. most of the commands / requests application can send to the terminal are sent in-band, by printing them to stdout. terminal can then reply by sending data to stdin. as Deno allows programs to print arbitrary data to stdout and read from stdin without requiring any permissions or doing any filtering, malicious code can send arbitrary commands to the terminal. itâs usually okay, because terminals wonât, like, execute shell commands just because stdout told them to, youâre supposed to be able to freely cat files without risking arbitrary code execution. itâs markedly less okay if you allow malicious code to do whatever with the terminal and then print a prompt on the same exact terminal.

you could, like, hide the prompt by messing with terminal colors. (this one got closed in 2026 because the permission prompt is âpartially visibleâ (you can see an emoji) and âAI agents tend toâ change terminal colors, so thatâs a âvalid use-caseâ)

or trick the user into pre-feeding approval into stdin.

or trick the terminal into feeding approval into stdin as a response to some request. (terminal wonât ever send Enter to stdin to avoid executing commands, but âpress Enter to continueâ is common enough to not be suspicious; the user never sees the actual prompt). hereâs an asciicast of that, I think it looks quite cool.

the specific issue on the screencast is long patched; the issue with terminal colors is not. that doesnât really matter because the real issue is using an attacker-controlled channel for security-sensitive information. itâs like executing attacker-controlled JS code on a webpage and then asking for password on the same page. you canât know that the page is in a safe state, so you canât trust any input.

even if Deno manages to patch every single issue with the âstandardâ escape codes, you never know which non-standard codes even exist out there. many terminals have some, itâs impossible to predict how they will interact with your prompt.

(aside: how come sudo can do it then? the difference is that sudo asks for the password first, before running any other code. to trick sudo that way youâd need to fuck up terminal state before you even type sudo, and do it quietly enough that you donât notice it while you type it. if some terminal allows it, Iâd consider it a bug in the terminal)

the --allow-run problem

so, thereâs a weird thing with this command I wrote above (Iâll copy it here for reference):

shell deno run --allow-read=/tmp/dir --allow-run=uname code.ts

what does --allow-run=uname even mean? itâs not like programs have canonical names, itâs not org.gnu.coreutils.uname, itâs not even /nix/store/8k1dmzr3gwzqdgw45nzj76902ca7g1is-coreutils-full-9.5/bin/uname. itâs just a shortcut for âlook at all the directories in PATH one-by-one to see if you can find uname thereâ.

you can set environment variables for the child process without needing any extra permissions, so what if we just

$ cat t.ts const command = new Deno.Command("uname", { // my current working directory, can be anything env: { 'PATH': '/tmp/tmp.7ofmKaNW83' }, }); const { code, stdout, stderr } = command.outputSync(); console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(stdout)); $ cat uname #!/bin/sh printf lol $ deno run --allow-run=uname t.ts lol

yeah.

once again, we have a pretty and convenient interface that doesnât really make sense from the security standpoint. it would be nice if programs were uniquely identified by their names, but theyâre not, and pretending they are leads to security holes.

funnily enough, I didnât even think that this issue would be there when I poked at Deno for the first time, so I havenât reported it until now (spoiler alert: this is a comment on a GitHub issue that I created for the problem Iâll explain below).

so letâs imagine we fixed that. itâs not that hard, we can force PATH to be whatever it was when the runtime started, or always require fully-qualified paths, or prompt with a fully-qualified path before running. are we safe now?

lol no of course weâre not. while PATH decides which executable gets run, dynamically-linked executables (so, like, most executables) require dynamic loader to actually start. dynamic loader is a program that, well, loads the executable into memory, finds its dependencies and does a bunch of other fun stuff we wonât get into. the important part is that dynamic loader is configurable via environment variables. you can probably see where this is going now.

LD_PRELOAD instructs the dynamic loader to load specific dynamic library when loading executables. dynamic libraries can execute arbitrary code on load. we can just pass LD_PRELOAD and weâve completely escaped the sandbox once again:

$ cat t.c #include <stdio.h> // ask dynamic loader to run this function on load time pretty please __attribute__((constructor)) void lol() { puts("lol"); } $ cat t.ts const command = new Deno.Command("uname", { // ask dynamic loader to load our evil library env: { 'LD_PRELOAD': '/tmp/tmp.7ofmKaNW83/liblol.so' }, }); const { code, stdout, stderr } = command.outputSync(); console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(stdout)); $ gcc -fPIC -shared t.c -o liblol.so $ # that's the real uname now! $ deno run --allow-run=uname t.ts lol Linux

I reported this some time ago and now they patched it by disallowing to set environment variables starting with LD_. this, once again, fixes a specific issue while ignoring the larger problem: âpermission to run a single commandâ is mostly not a useful concept. (you can do secure interfaces by allowing to run a single command, like git-over-SSH does, but generally both the environment and the command need to be prepared to handle it)

say, for example, our script wants to invoke the $EDITOR so user can edit some data (think git commit messages). thatâs a very natural permission request, and itâs also an unmitigated disaster because most editors are configurable enough for running one to be a full sandbox escape. itâs easy for user to absent-mindedly grant --allow-run=vim (âwell, sure, I want to edit this file!â), but then the script can just set VIMINIT='!rm -rf /*' and oops, all my files are gone. most programs are configurable, often in some ways you wonât think about (like LD_PRELOAD), and attacker controls the execution enviornment. âpatch some specific ways to configure programsâ is not the solution, the solution is to sandbox all the code, not just JS code.

when we discussed all this stuff in GitHub issues, a Deno developer wrote:

The main thing it protects you against is malicious code that isn't smart enough.

upon reading this, I was enlightened.

conclusions

deno tries really hard to do what the operating system should be doing. it emulates syscall filtering by filtering standard library calls. unfortunately, this breaks down the second you need to run code that doesnât use Deno standard library. it also uses somewhat flawed approach to permission management that looks good (wow, runtime prompts! omg, I can just --allow-run=uname!), but introduces security risks. in doing this, it implicitly requires user to understand all the implications of various permissions and their combinations, which can be really hard.

Deno process is not actually sandboxed, it only pretends it is. I didnât mention some more boring issues like âDeno doesnât prevent you from following symlinks that lead outside of the sandboxâ because they all just boil down to this simple one: the process is not sandboxed.

one can argue that this pseudo-sandboxing is better than nothing: after all, not all the malicious code is smart enough. I disagree: Deno permissions give a false sense of security and can lure someone into running untrusted code without proper sandboxing.

itâs possible that you can use Deno sandboxing safely if you:

never use more dangerous permissions like --allow-run, even with =cmd, that includes --allow-env, even --allow-env=VAR, for setting environment variables is memory unsafe and can affect libc functions, preferrably run with --no-prompt so your terminal canât be tricked, are careful about symlinks in directories you --allow-{read,write} to, are not concerned with resource exhaustion: thereâre zero permissions required to burn CPU or allocate memory.

in particular, you may be safe if youâre running untrusted code with no permissions at all in a non-interactive context and use some other mechanism to control resource consumption.

I still donât think you should do it. this path is riddled with footguns because youâre executing untrusted code in a fully-privileged process, and the moment you need some OS interactions youâre no longer running code âwith no permissions at allâ. you should not try to figure out which stdlib APIs can lead to a sandbox escape when combined. you should just use a proper sandbox.

Iâm not a fan of Denoâs security model.

so what do we do?

just bwrap untrusted shit.

also, please: donât harass Deno developers. we have a technical disagreement, but no technical disagreement was ever solved by harassment. this post is explicitly not an invitation to do it. Iâve already explained my point of view to them, they disagreed, and thatâs okay. you donât need to reiterate it, it wonât help anybody.

item.title: A Little Snitch for Windows
item.description:
Asks once, remembers

The first time an app tries to connect, you see who made it, where it's going and on which port. Click Allow or Block, for the whole app or just one address, host or domain, and keep it forever or only until the app quits.

Most firewalls only watch what comes in. PacketHound sniffs out what goes out: the first time an app tries to connect to the internet, it asks you to Allow or Block, and remembers your answer.

PacketHound turns Windows Firewall into an "ask me first" firewall for outgoing connections, without drowning you in questions about Windows itself.

Windows' own components are allowed automatically, so you're only asked about the apps you installed, not about hundreds of system services.

A program only counts as Windows if it lives in a Windows folder, is owned by the system and carries a valid Microsoft Windows signature. Copying malware into System32 doesn't get it a free pass.

Malware loves PowerShell, curl, certutil, mshta and rundll32 for downloading payloads. PacketHound still asks before those connect, even though they're part of Windows.

No kernel driver, nothing hidden. Every decision is an ordinary Windows Firewall rule you can see in wf.msc, and it keeps working even when PacketHound is closed.

Prompts appear on top without taking keyboard focus, so you can't answer one by accident while you're typing.

Flip any app between Allow and Block with one switch. Search, sort, see when each decision was made, and clear out rules for programs you've uninstalled.

The activity log shows every blocked attempt with its hostname, port and what happened next. Not sure yet? Decide later, and come back to it from the Rules tab.

Click any picture to see it full size.

No drivers, no background service of its own: PacketHound builds on the firewall that's already part of Windows.

PacketHound switches Windows Firewall's outgoing default to block, so a program without a rule can't reach the internet.

Windows logs each blocked attempt. PacketHound watches that log, checks whether the program is part of Windows, and allows it quietly if so.

For everything else you get a prompt showing the app, its publisher and where it's connecting. Your answer becomes a firewall rule, for the whole app or one destination, kept forever or until the app quits.

Yes. There's no trial, no account and no adverts. If you find it useful, you can buy me a coffee.

Yes. The full source code is on GitHub, under the GNU General Public License v3. You don't have to take our word for what PacketHound does: you (or someone you trust) can read exactly how it works, or build it yourself.

No. PacketHound doesn't collect anything and has no analytics. It looks up the names of the servers apps try to reach (a normal DNS lookup), so it can show you "example.com" instead of a bare IP address, and once a week it asks this website whether there's a newer version. That request contains nothing about you or your PC, and you can turn it off. See the privacy page.

That's Microsoft SmartScreen's warning for programs it hasn't seen many people download yet. Click More info, then Run anyway. You can check the file is exactly the one published here by comparing its SHA-256 checksum with the one on the download page.

Changing Windows Firewall settings and reading the Security event log both require them, so Windows asks you to confirm when you start PacketHound. If you let it start when you sign in, it starts without asking.

Your rules keep working: they're ordinary Windows Firewall rules. When you exit, PacketHound asks whether to keep blocking apps that don't have a rule yet. Either way, apps you blocked stay blocked.

Open PacketHound from the notification area, find the app on the Rules tab and flip its switch to Allow. Or delete the rule, and PacketHound will ask about the app again next time.

Yes. Right-click the tray icon and choose Pause protection, for 5 minutes, 15 minutes, an hour, or until you turn it back on. A timed pause turns protection back on by itself. While paused, apps without a rule can connect freely; your Block rules still apply.

Its first connection was blocked before you could answer, and some installers give up straight away. Click the notification PacketHound shows after you allow it (or right-click the tray icon › Pause protection › For 5 minutes) and run the installer again. Protection turns back on by itself. Next time, PacketHound recognises that installer and lets it through before it starts.

The app stays blocked and is listed on the Rules tab under Waiting for your decision, where you can decide any time. PacketHound also asks again after 10 minutes if the app is still running, or the next time it connects.

Yes. PacketHound uses Windows Firewall, which works alongside Microsoft Defender and most antivirus software. If a third-party security suite has replaced Windows Firewall with its own, PacketHound can't work, because there's no Windows Firewall to manage.

From Windows Settings › Apps. The uninstaller asks whether to delete PacketHound's firewall rules, then puts Windows Firewall's settings back the way they were before you installed it.

Open an issue on PacketHound's GitHub page (you'll need a free GitHub account). For a bug, say which version of PacketHound and Windows you're using and what happened. The log in C:\ProgramData\PacketHound often helps.

Free for Windows 10 and 11. Installs in a minute, uninstalls cleanly.

item.title: Goldman Sachs is pulling Claude Code from its bankers and traders
item.description:
Goldman Sachs has restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its engineers, cutting off traders and bankers who used the tools to track client flows and build market models. The bank barred its Hong Kong bankers from Claude in April and is now a lead underwriter on Anthropic's IPO.

Most traders and bankers at Goldman Sachs can no longer use AI coding tools at work. Internal guidance updated in October restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to the bank's engineers, Bloomberg News reported, following a review of productivity and risk concerns.

Strats, who work across trading, quantitative research and software engineering, still have access, according to a second person familiar with the matter.

The change has frustrated some traders, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. They had been using the tools to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and put together written and graphic material. Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra said the bank makes certain AI tools available to staff "to determine the best use cases" across the firm.

Argenti was praising trader-built tools in July

As recently as July, chief information officer Marco Argenti was talking up "vibe coding" by Goldman's non-technical employees. He told Bloomberg that traders and bankers had built tools with AI and passed them to the firm's engineers, of whom there are about 12,000, to be improved.

That arrangement let the people closest to a problem build a first version without waiting for engineering time. It also meant thousands of employees without engineering training were running software that writes and executes code, on the same machines they use to handle client information.

At a conference in Turin last month, Argenti described Goldman's AI adoption in waves and said developers, more than 12,000 of the bank's roughly 47,000 staff, had made up the first. The October guidance limits the coding agents to that group.

Goldman restricted Claude in Hong Kong in April

In April, Goldman removed Claude from its internal AI platform for bankers in Hong Kong. The Financial Times reported that the bank had read its contract with Anthropic strictly, and an Anthropic spokesperson said Claude had never been officially supported in Hong Kong. ChatGPT and Gemini remained available there. JPMorgan removed Claude from its Hong Kong approved list in June.

The Hong Kong restriction was based on location and contract terms, and the new one is based on role. Goldman's in-house AI assistant, which uses models from several companies, is still available across the firm. The restriction applies to third-party agents that can write and run code by themselves.

Goldman is still working closely with Anthropic

Earlier this year, Goldman said Anthropic engineers had spent six months at the bank helping build Claude-based agents for trade accounting and client onboarding. Those agents sit in the back office and are run by Goldman's engineering teams.

Goldman and Morgan Stanley are also the lead underwriters on Anthropic's IPO, according to the S-1 filed October 26. Anthropic is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT before the end of November, as we reported last week. Over the next few weeks, Goldman's bankers will be marketing shares in a company whose coding agent most of them are no longer allowed to use.

Why a coding agent is riskier on a trading desk

Claude Code reads files, writes programs and runs them, typically with the same access as the person using it. Code an engineer writes with it usually goes through review, testing and deployment controls before it reaches anything important. A script a trader builds to watch client flows can end up in daily use without going through any of those.

Banks are also required to keep information barriers between groups, for example between bankers working on deals and traders who could profit from knowing about them. Goldman built its internal AI platform around controls like these. A tool a trader puts together with an agent wasn't designed with them in mind, and engineers can only check it if someone sends it their way.

There is also the matter of whether anyone understands the code. Last month a Meta engineer said he now ships code he can't fully account for, and writing software is his job. A trader using an agent to model positions is less likely to know how that code handles unusual cases, which on a trading desk can mean losses.

Cost may also have played a part. Agent usage is billed by the token, and several companies that gave agents to everyone have seen spending climb. Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard after employees ran agents on pointless tasks to move up it, and Accenture now funds $29 a month of Claude per employee. Bloomberg's sources said productivity was part of Goldman's review.

Barclays is moving in the other direction

Barclays said in October that it expects half its developers to be using Claude Code by the end of the year, and three weeks later named developers among 5,000 job cuts. Like Goldman, it is giving coding agents to engineers. Unlike Goldman, it is also using them to reduce how many engineers it employs.

Banks have tightened agent access in other places this fall. JPMorgan and Schwab are blocking outside agents from customer accounts, and Goldman has now set limits on which of its own employees can use them.

Our take

At State of AI, we think Goldman was right to restrict the tools and wrong in how it went about it.

A trading floor is a bad place for unreviewed code written by people who can't read it, and the information barrier problem would be reason enough on its own. Requiring that agent-written code come from people trained to review it is a sensible rule for a regulated business.

Goldman's own CIO was promoting traders' AI-built tools in July, though. Withdrawing access through a guideline update, with no replacement mentioned in Bloomberg's reporting, tells the traders who found good uses that they were the risk. Their complaints point to work the engineering team could take on, and Goldman would get more out of collecting them than out of waiting for them to fade.

Leaders at other companies should settle who owns agent-built code before handing agents out. When someone outside engineering builds a tool with Claude Code or Copilot, a named engineer should take responsibility for it before it touches production data.

Existing controls should cover code an agent writes. Information barriers, data entitlements and software approval rules still apply when the code came from a prompt.

And when a tool is taken away, it's worth recording what people were using it for. Goldman's traders were watching client flows and modeling positions, and they will still need to do both.

item.title: Playing Zork 1 on a CP/M emulator on Linux (2021)
item.description:
Playing Zork 1 on a CP/M emulator on Linux

This article is about using the z80pack Z80 emulator to run CP/M on Linux, and then using the CP/M implementation to run Zork 1. I've chosen Zork 1 for this example because it's a non-trivial program that, nonetheless, uses only plain text input and output. Running something like WordStar might be more illustrative, but it raises terminal-related problems that I don't want to get into in this simple example. However, I will discuss this subject at the end of the article.

Note:There is absolutely no practical reason to play Zork using a CP/M emulator. There are many better ways to play Zork -- should you want to -- on a modern computer. A reason -- probably the only reason -- for using a CP/M emulator is to become familiar with CP/M in general, with a view to building your own Z80-based retro computer.

Zork is an early example of what these days is called "interactive fiction", but was know as a "text adventure" back in the days when all computing was text-based. Zork accepts simple instructions like "take axe" and "look at box" as input to what is essentially a puzzle-solving exercise. CP/M is an early operating system, originally for microcomputers with floppy drives, but eventually for early hard drives. Almost nobody under the age of 50 remembers using CP/M when it was the latest and greatest, but its legacy lives on in MS-DOS, which it inspired.

CP/M was originally developed for 8080 microprocessors, but was more widely used with the Z80. To run CP/M on Linux, probably the easiest approach is to use a Z80 emulator.

In this article I'll outline how to obtain and build z80pack and some CP/M tools for Linux, how to set up virtual disks to store the Zork files, and how to run the program from the CP/M command prompt.

I'm assuming that you're familiar with Linux, and willing to work with command-line tools. I also assume you have at least an inkling what CP/M is.

Installing z80pack

I don't think that z80pack is routinely available in standard Linux repositories -- if it is, it might not be up-to-date. You'll need to Download the source and build it.

Unpack the source into any convenient directory. I'm using $HOME/lib/z80pack-1.37.

Compile the core:

$ cd ~/lib/z80pack-1.37/cpmsim/srcsim $ make -f Makefile.linux

Compile the supporting tools:

$ cd ~/lib/z80pack-1.37/cpmsim/srctools $ make -f Makefile.linux

Test that the installation is basically functional, by starting CP/M 3:

$ cd ~/lib/z80pack-1.37/cpmsim $ ./cpm3

Note that cpm3 is just a script, that runs ./cpmsim after copying relevant disks from the disk image library (more on this below).

Build and install cpmtools

cpmtools is a set of utilities for managing CP/M disk images. It can list disk image contents, and copy files to and from them. We'll need this for copying program files and data from the host system to CP/M.

cpmtools is available in various Linux repositories, but I found that the repository version for my (Fedora 31) system did not work reliably. It's easy to build from source, however.

Download the source. Unpack the archive, run ./configure, then make, the sudo make install. The default installation is in /usr/local/bin which may, or may not, be in your $PATH.

How z80pack handles disks

z80pack uses files (images) to represent physical disks, as most virtualisation software does. The files have a structure that is in some senses a representation of a physical disk, so the tools that manipulate them (that is, the utilities from the cpmtools package) need to know about physical disk structure. The cpmtools utilities assume, by default, a 720kB, 8-inch floppy disk -- this is fine for many purposes. It will be fine for running Zork 1, in fact, but I'll explain how to create a hard disk image anyway, because it's likely that you'll need to at some point.

cpmsim looks for disk images in the "./disks" directory by default. That is, it looks in a directory relative to the current working directory. It supports, essentially, six disk devices: floppy drives A: to D:, and hard disks I: and P:. It expects to find images for these disks as files drivea.dsk, driveb.dsk, etc. If these image files are not all present, cpmsim will still start -- it will just respond as if there's no medium in the drive.

The minimum needed to boot CP/M 3 is the image disks/library/cpm3-1.dsk as drive A: However, there are some useful utilities on the second disk of the CP/M set, destined for drive B: So:

$ cp disks/library/cpm3-1.dsk disks/drivea.dsk $ cp disks/library/cpm3-2.dsk disks/driveb.dsk

You should now be able to run ./cpmsim, and you'll find that only drives A: and B: are available.

Let's create a 4Mb hard disk to serve as drive I: (CP/M-3 actually supports up to 500Mb, but 4Mb is more than enough for this example).

$ /usr/local/bin/mkfs.cpm -fz80pack-hd disks/drivei.dsk

In this command, z80pack-hd refers to a set of physical disk parameters that are stored in the file /usr/local/share/diskdefs. Omitting this parameter will result in the creation of a 720kB floppy disk image.

Obtaining and installing the Zork 1 program files

Like all the original Infocom games, the Zork series exists in a kind of legal limbo, and probably will continue to do so for at least another ten years. It isn't clear who now owns the intellectual property, and what redistribution terms, if any, exist. Consequently, although it's easy to get hold of the CP/M version of Zork 1, there is no "official" source, and I'm not going to be hosting it myself. I got my copy from here.

The CP/M version of Zork 1 consists of two files: the binary ZORK1.COM and the data file ZORK1.DAT. The data file is actually a z-machine program, and can be played using various alternative z-machine emulators, like frotz. These two files need to be placed into the same disk image, like this:

$ /usr/local/bin/cpmcp -fz80pack-hd disks/drivei.dsk ZORK1.COM 0: $ /usr/local/bin/cpmcp -fz80pack-hd disks/drivei.dsk ZORK1.DAT 0: Note:CP/M disks do not support subdirectories. Instead, they have numbered "user areas" which can be selected at the command prompt. In the commands above, we're copying to the default user area, area zero. Playing Zork 1

There is a slight complication related to the use of the "backspace" key in cpmsim. In general, Linux terminals and terminal emulators generate the DEL code (ASCII 127) when you hit the backspace key. The CP/M command prompt will respond to DEL and erase a character, but Zork 1 requires the more traditional "ctrl-h" (ASCII 8). You could still type "ctrl-h" explicitly to delete a character, but it's more elegant to set the terminal so that the backspace key actually generates a ctrl-h. With Gnome terminal, the relevant setting is in the "Compatibility" tab of the profile settings page. Other terminals and terminal emulators will have other ways to change this setting.

Having made this change, you'll probably have to tell the Linux terminal infrastructure about the new key mapping, or the backspace key won't work anywhere except in Zork. To do that:

$ stty erase ^H

The Linux shell should still work as normal, but the backspace key will be generating a different code. Now it should be very straightforward to run Zork 1:

$ ./cpmsim ... ... A> i: I> zork1 ZORK I: The Great Underground Empire Copyright 1982 by Infocom, Inc. All rights reserved. ZORK is a trademark of Infocom, Inc. Release 25 / Serial number 000000 West of House You are standing in an open field west of a white house, with a boarded front door. There is a small mailbox here. >open mailbox Opening the mailbox reveals a leaflet. >read leaflet (Taken) WELCOME TO ZORK ZORK is a game of adventure, danger, and low cunning. In it you will explore some of the most amazing territory ever seen by mortals. No computer should be without one! Copyright 1982 by Infocom, Inc. All rights reserved. ZORK is a trademark of Infocom, Inc.

... and away we go.

Further adventures with CP/M

CP/M was a hugely popular operating system in its day, and there is a massive amount of software available for it. Much of it is in a legally-uncertain position, as the Zork games are. However, the software is easy to obtain and, as "abandonware", using it for private and educational purposes is unlikely to upset anybody.

The "killer app" for CP/M was WordStar, and this rudimentary word processor is still available, and surprisingly widely used. Another honourable mention goes to Borland's Turbo Pascal -- an astonishingly good compiler, which used various tricks to get around the limited RAM (64k) that the Z80 could address.

All these applications are screen-based, rather than line-based; running them raises complications related to terminal handling. There was no universal way of doing terminal output in a CP/M application -- each application made its own provision. z80pack does not provide a terminal -- it just passes the output from the CP/M program to the terminal that is hosting it. Most Linux terminal emulators are broadly VT100-like, and if you configure CP/M software to use a VT100 or VT52 terminal, you'll probably get reasonable results.

Have you posted something in response to this page? Feel free to send a webmention to notify me, giving the URL of the blog or page that refers to this one.

item.title: Playing with the STM32MP2
item.description:
Playing with the STM32MP2 Record scratch

First off, an apology - this post is long overdue. I started writing it back even before the TCXO post, I think some time in December 2025. But then I ended up accidentally finding a silicon bug with security impacts (described later on in this post, and stay tuned for a blog from work on the bug in particular) that I had to keep quiet about until ST had a chance to review and put an advisory out, and there wasnât a whole lot I could publish about this project until then. Once that finally came out I got busy on other things.

Anyway, here we are. My long time readers will know that I like using STM32s and pairing them with FPGAs, and have got some pretty decent performance doing this, e.g. close to a Gbps of Ethernet bandwidth from the MCU to an FPGA-side RGMII MAC. Thereâs just one problem: the STM32H7 FMC needs a lot of pins - 30+ if you want all the chip selects and address lines. And theyâre not nicely located all on one side of the package either, that would be too easy. Theyâre all over the place.

Hereâs an example of what the FMC looks like on the TFBGA240 package for the H750.

And the TFBGA216 isnât any better, either.

For years, Iâve dreamed of a better way. My ultimate dream MCU, which doesnât exist because Iâm probably the only weirdo who would buy it, would be a 1 GHz Cortex-M7 or M85, probably made on TSMC 28LP, with a megabyte of NOR flash or ReRAM, a megabyte of SRAM, an RGMII MAC, multiple FPGA-style I/O banks with independent VCCIO rails, and an AXI Chip2Chip SERDES block that I could use for directly integrating with FPGA-based peripherals using only two differential pairs.

The STM32H735 paired with an external FPGA over FMC got close, but was annoying to use on a low-cost board (e.g. 4 layer batch fab) because the FMC is almost impossible to route on those constraints. Some other STM32H7 parts like the H75x line are available in an 0.8mm package which is doable (painfully) on batch fab design rules, but these have a lower max CPU speed (480 vs 550 MHz) and this is really just kicking the can down the road a bit rather than fully solving the problem. Youâre still burning a ton of pins.

A fast M7 with PCIe would almost be what I want (PCIe isnât exactly AXI, but bridging them is totally doable), but nobody makes those either. You can get Cortex-Râs with PCIe, which I seriously considered (and still want to check out) but it would still be a big jump from the familiar STM32 peripheral set. And a lot of these parts either donât have crypto acceleration or security-by-obscurity lock up the docs to the crypto accelerator, which is an absolute dealbreaker for me.

Enter the STM32MP2

But then ST came out with the STM32MP2 line. This is a full applications processor SoC with a dual Cortex-A35, some slower auxiliary processors like an M33 and a M0+, a full GPU/NPU I may play with one day, and â most interestingly to me â a 5 Gbps SERDES with PIPE interface that could be configured to operate as either PCIe gen1/2 x1 or USB 3 depending on which internal protocol IP you connect to it (thereâs a register bit to mux them). It also kept most of the same familiar STM32 peripherals I already had lots of libraries for and experience working with, so the learning curve getting spun up on it would be short - including the same AES-GCM and TRNG IPs that I already had drivers for, and were reasonably well documented.

Itâs quite a beast with far more computing power than I needed, but I did want to have a part in my back pocket I could pull out for future designs that needed more oomph. And the PCIe would potentially allow easy memory mapping of an FPGA from firmware via only two differential pairs.

Thereâs just one problem: the STM32MP2 was clearly designed to run Linux, and the vendor BSPs included all kinds of u-boot, TrustZone, etc. stuff that I didnât care about. I just wanted a big microcontroller that could run a simple RTOS or even a while(1) { doStuff(); } event loop.

How hard could it be?

So I decided to see if I could convince the MP2 that it was, in fact, just a very fast MCU with some oddball peripherals like PCIe and LPDDR PHYs that garden-variety MCUs donât have.

The goals of the experiment were:

Build entirely with upstream aarch64 / arm g++ and binutils, no vendor SDKs or HALs Get code running on the A35s plus the M33 auxiliary core Donât use external DDR (this is a massive board complexity adder and I wanted to stay as close to MCU-level BOM/PCB design effort levels as possible); all code and data lives in on-die SRAM Donât use trustzone, uboot, or any other baggage. Just run a simple event loop in EL3 out of the initial âfirst stage boot loaderâ (FSBL) flash image and have that be the entire firmware. Get PCIe working to an FPGA under these constraints

I bought a STM32MP257 development board (STM32MP257F-EV1) and started out the same as I would with any other new STM32 part: added a linker script and header to stm32-cpp with the addresses of the peripherals that used the same register interface as other STM32 parts I already had supported in the library. The only difference was that the image base address was in SRAM rather than flash.

M33 bringup

Then I built a simple LED blinky firmware for the Cortex-M33 auxiliary core and loaded it over JTAG just like I would for a regular STM32. There were a few false starts but I got a blinky running fairly quickly. Achievement #1 unlocked: I can talk to the chip and poke registers.

The next milestone was to actually boot the same blinky from flash. It took some digging through example code and wikis to figure out all of the fine points (for example, the internal SRAM is mapped at four different physical addresses with different TrustZone etc settings, but the boot ROM only lets you boot from one of them). Before too long I had a tool that took a flat binary RAM image and bolted on the necessary FSBL headers for the STM32MP2 boot ROM to load it from flash and execute. Then I made a little flasher utility that could be loaded into SRAM and would write an image from another SRAM location to flash, bootstrapping the whole process. Achievement #2 unlocked: the chip is booting from nonvolatile memory and doesnât need to be loaded over JTAG each boot.

A few things to keep in mind when preparing the FSBL image:

Place your FSBL-M code image in RETRAM, specifically within the boot alias at 0x0e08_0000. Your stack and initial globals must live in RETRAM too, but on the D-side bus alias at 0x3008_0000. Your memory map must ensure that the physical memory of these doesnât overlap, i.e. if you have code at 0x0e08_4141 you cannot also have data at 0x3008_4141. The linker script gymnastics to handle .text, .data, and .bss going to different logical addresses but also not colliding with one another are an adventure but not too bad once you realize how it works. There are two slots for FSBL-M images, primary at flash offset 0x0000_0000 and fallback at 0x0004_0000

This firmware booted in âM33-TDâ mode, in which the boot ROM immediately transfers control to the M33 after loading the FSBL image, and the M33 has full TrustZone privileges. I chose this over âA35-TDâ (in which the A35 boots first) mostly because I wanted to do a staged bring-up of the platform and not have my first time working with the SoC also be my first time bringing up a bare metal Cortex-A.

I continued along the same way I would with any other new STM32 platform for a bit, bringing up a serial console, enabling caches, configuring the PLLs and clock tree, dumping a bunch of platform information to the console on boot, etc.

The code is all on my GitHub but a quick summary of what you need to do for bare metal bringup in M33-TD is as follows. None of the SoC setup code here requires custom assembly, it can all be done in C/C++ except for CPU configuration stuff like enabling/disabling interrupts or the FPU when youâre ready to do that.

Enable the VDDIO monitor for VDDIO1â¦4. Wait until they report valid, then tell the PWR theyâre ready. Without this step, most of your IOs wonât be available. Optional: Enable writing to backup SRAM (by default itâs gated by POR/brownout detection to avoid glitches when the Vcore domain drops out of regulation) Set SYSCFG.VDERAMCR to use the video encoder RAM as processor memory since weâre not using the video block Enable all of the SRAMs (SYSRAM, SRAM1, SRAM2, backup SRAM, VDERAM, LPSRAM1â¦3) in the RCC. Thereâs a lot of them. Set the RISAB SECCFGR register settings to enable secure domain code to access SRAM1/2 and VDERAM. By default these arenât accessible to EL3 secure mode. Weâre writing all of our code in EL3 secure so we want everything allocated there. Initialize the clock tree. Thereâs a LOT of different clocks, you can look at my code to see the details of how I set it up. Enable and invalidate the M33âs I-side and D-side L1 caches On to the A35

Then it came time to get the A35 running, which I had to do before playing with the PCIe because the M33âs memory map did not allow it to talk to the PCIe BAR region â annoying, but something I could live with if the M33 is mostly acting as a management processor and all our application code is on the A35.

I had previously avoided working with Cortex-Aâs because the overhead involved in getting them set up was a lot higher.

First, once you have the A35 image in flash, you need to actually start it. Figuring this out took quite a bit of reading of various third party library code and such, the datasheet didnât make it obvious. The basic steps are:

Check the DSTATE of the CPU in PWR.CPU1D1SR. It should be in STANDBY. Send a SEV via EXTI1.RPR3 to wake up the CPU Reset the CPU via RCC.C1RSTCSETR Set EXTI1.SWIER3 Wait until PWR.CPU1D1SR reports the CPU is in HOLD_BOOT state Release the CPU to boot by setting RCC.CPUBOOTCR to 2

The FSBL-A image in flash (at offset 0x0008_0000 for primary and 0x000c_0000 for fallback) itself then is launched in parallel on both cores in the cluster simultaneously in aarch64 mode (although there is a fuse you can blow to boot in aarch32 mode instead if you wanted to for some reason). The first part of this initialization does have to be done in assembly because thereâs a bunch of stuff needed that pokes hardware registers and initializes the stack etc.

Note also that this image has to be in flash: even if you have code executing on the M33 already, there does not appear to be a good way to just have the M33 dump an image into SYSRAM and have the A35 execute it: when the A35 is released to boot the ROM will check strap pins and load the image from the specified location (in my case SPI NOR flash); even though the M33 is already running the A35 is going to re-run the boot ROM.

The image should be loaded to the boot/secure SYSRAM alias (0x0e00_0000) The image begins with a jump to the reset vector, then a bunch of padding so the exception table is aligned at a 2 kB boundary as required by hardware. Thereâs probably some room to optimize here, right now that space is wasted but it should be possible to fit most of the low level initialization in there too. The exception table is repeated four times for EL0, higher exception levels, and synchronous exceptions from lower levels. You have 128 bytes for each handler in the table itself, theyâre not vectored like in M. But you can jump to external code if you need more space. Iâm not a huge fan of this, I prefer the Cortex-M NVIC. Maybe this saves a branch instruction and reduces interrupt latency slightly? Anyway, for early testing I just set every exception handler to be an infinite loop. Register values are undefined at startup (whatever the boot ROM left them at), so I clear them all to zero before going any further. Exception status registers also need to be cleared Initialize the floating point unit and NEON/vector units if you plan to use them. My current startup code doesnât do this yet since I only do integer stuff, but if you plan to ever use floats it needs to happen here. Point VBAR_EL3 to the exception table so if we throw an exception we donât end up back in the boot ROMâs exception handler Enable cache coherency in CPUECTLR_EL1

At this point the lowest levels of the core are set up, but we donât know which core weâre on yet. So the next step is to read MPIDR_EL1 and figure out which one weâre on, since the subsequent steps vary depending on which core weâre on.

If weâre on core 0:

Initialize the stack pointer. Now we have a valid environment to start runing C++ code, with one caveat: we cannot call memcpy yet, because until the MMU is enabled everything is considered âdeviceâ memory and the newlib aarch64 memcpy implementation will try to ldp from unaligned addresses which isnât allowed from device memory. Create initial page tables. My mapping has a total of three page tables, one level 1 (512x 1GB pages covering the entire memory map) and then two level 2 (512x 2 MB pages) under it. One of them covers the on chip SRAM and PCIe BAR region, the other covers the peripherals, OCTOSPI, and FMC. In my mapping, everything is set up as cacheable except MMIO ranges and the translation is 1:1 (VA = PA) since I am only using the MMU to control NX and caching attributes (I wish I could get a Cortex-M MPU here). I intentionally left the pages covering the boot ROM region as unmapped since itâs mapped at 0x0000_0000 and I want null pointers to segfault, not read random stuff from the ROM. Once page tables are set up, turn on the MMU. Call BSP hooks to do any other power, clock, etc. initialization required before application code starts. This includes configuring and starting the main PLL for the A35 itself. Call __libc_init_array to run constructors for global objects Set a flag to tell core 1 that weâre done with the system init

If weâre on core 1:

Initialize the stack pointer Spin until core 0 finishes setup Set up the MMU pointing at the same page table as core 0. Page tables are 2 kB each and we have limited on chip RAMâ¦ we donât want to burn two page tables worth of memory unless thereâs a good reason to have different mappings on each core. (This is one of the reasons I like Cortex-Mâs, the MPU has far less baggage than the Aâs MMU. But nobody makes Mâs with PCIe so here we are.)

On either core:

Invalidate and enable the instruction and data caches Call the CoreMain() function provided by the BSP, passing the core number as the argument, so application code can start running. All cores are set up. What now?

Youâll notice that I havenât said much about the DDR. Thatâs because I donât plan to use it. Itâs a Synopsys DDR3L/DDR4/LPDDR4 controller that requires a blob plus annoying PCB layout for all the data lines, uses a bunch of power, and is just all around overkill. The whole point of switching from the STM32H735 to the MP2 was to replace the parallel memory bus with PCIe and using DDR would negate most of those benefits.

Anywayâ¦ at this point, you basically have a STM32H7 on steroids:

808 kB of SRAM in the MP2 vs the 564 kB of my usual H735. No flash though, so you have to fit code + data in the SRAM (or XIP from external SPI flash which is slow - but you do have 2x 32KB L1$ and a unified 512 kB L2$ so if your firmware fits in that it should be pretty fast? I havenât tried yet) Dual A35s at 1.5 GHz instead of an M7 at 500 MHz. So 6x more clock cycles available, but a less performant core IPC wise (the A35 is 1.7 DMIPS/MHz, vs the M7 is 2.14 DMIPS/MHz) thus probably only ~4x faster on a typical workload No ITCM/DTCM so anything that misses in L1$ wonât be single cycle. This is another thing I dislike about Aâs. I use TCMs on the STM32H7 heavily for all of my fast stuff. 400 MHz M33 and 200 MHz M0+ auxiliary cores

The MP2 has the same FMC hard IP as the H735, so if I wanted to be silly I could interface it to the FPGA just like the H7. But then why go through all this trouble to bring up the more complex SoC? We want to do PCIe otherwise thereâs no point.

Bringing up the PCIe

The STM32MP257F-EV1 has a mini PCIe slot meant for a wifi card or something, but I found some adapters to convert it to M.2. This allowed me to interface to a random old NVMe SSD for early testing, and to an M.2 FPGA module later on.

The datasheet provides some initial breadcrumbs on configuring things. We need to enable the COMBOPHY and PCIe IPs in the RCC like usual, then poke SYSCFG.COMBOPHYCR1 to specify whether weâre using the external reference clock (typically 100 MHz but the PLL can be configured for other multiplier/divide combinations) or using an internally generated clock from the RCC.

Once everything is turned on, itâs just a matter of configuring COMBOPHYCR2 to enable PCIe mode, poke COMBOPHYCR3 to calibrate the controlled impedance drivers/terminations, then wait for the other internal housekeeping to complete and the PHY to report everything is ready to go.

Finally, poke SYSCFG.PCIECR to specify the initial bus/device ID and enable the LTSSM so we can actually train the link, toggle PERST to the peripheral, and wait for SYSCFG.PCIESR1 to report successful training. Somewhat shockingly, thereâs no firmware blob or weird setup flow. It just works and trains the link with only a handful of register pokes.

Or at least, I thought it did. After some issues attempting to enumerate the bus I found it was flapping and retraining constantly.

PHY level debug

Luckily I have a fast scope and ngscopeclient can decode PCIe and PCIe link training, so I went to work.

Looking at the startup process, everything seemed fine. The link trained up into L0 without any problems, then even passed a few TLPs before dropping into Recovery.RcvrLock, recovering for a bit, then dropping again. After that it stayed up for a while, dropped, and stayed down until the end of the waveform.

But why was it dropping? The first question was which side of the link was initiating the drop. It was pretty clear after zooming in that the STM32 was dropping (transitioning from idles in L0 to sending training sets) the first time, for no obvious reason while the link partner was still sending valid idles. So the problem was at least being detected, if not caused, on the STM32MP2.

I wondered if it might be signal integrity problems. So I fired up a quick eye pattern of both legs of the link. The RX lane (peripheral to STM32) looked fine. A bit overequalized since it was short and I was probing right at the mini-PCIe connector, but wide open with over 200 mV of eye height.

The TX (STM32 to peripheral) eye looked like nothing I had ever seen before. It was clear and wide open most of the time, but the entire eye was closed with a pretty uniform 1e-4 BER. Iâm used to seeing eyes that are squished horizontally due to jitter, vertically due to noise or reflections, etc but in such a scenario itâs usually consistent, the eye wonât have clear top and bottom bars or rising/falling edges.

The only thing I could think of was something intermittent. Maybe the signal is fine most of the time, the link comes up, then something happens - a noise burst, maybe - that blanks it out briefly before it comes back.

So I looked at the second, longer drop in the same waveform. This one was weirder: the link was fine then all of a sudden out of nowhere, the STM32MP2 started sending absolute nonsense - bit patterns that decoded as invalid scrambler values or sometimes not even well-formed 8b10b symbols at all! Then 40 Î¼s or so later the link partner noticed and went into re-training.

When I zoomed in further looking at just a few symbols on either side of the link drop, the problem immediately jumped out at me. Look at the relative phases of the purple Threshold_5 signal (a simple thresholding of the analog waveform) and the green squarewave below it (a clock recovered from the analog waveform by a DSP PLL).

At left, everything is happy. The recovered clock edges are 90Â° phased to the data allowing it to be cleanly sampled with plenty of setup and hold margin. But right about the middle of the screen, things start going sideways, literally. By the end of the D15.2 symbol the clock edge is only about 58 ps after the data edge (instead of the ideal 200ps setup/hold window for a 400ps UI at 2.5 GT/s). And by the end of the D11.7 the clock and data are on top of each other leaving no setup/hold window at all and the protocol decode starts seeing bit errors.

Both the DSP and real physical CDR PLL have limited bandwidth, so if theyâre handed this large a phase shift in <20 UI thereâs no way they will be able to keep up (although they will try).

Plotting TIE (time interval error, essentially the difference between where the CDR PLL expects a UI boundary to be compared to the actual level crossing in the real waveform) for the RX side shows pretty uniform jitter without any weird artifacts. But the TX side shows TIE jumping all over the place, railing at Â± 200 ps (half a UI - the max error possible before the edge is considered to be part of the next UI) and the CDR slewing frantically over 30 MHz above and below the nominal data rate trying and failing to stay synced.

Putting all the evidence together, itâs pretty clear that the SERDES PLL in the COMBOPHY is losing lock intermittently. Everything is fine for a while then something happens internally within the SERDES and the PLL VCO starts jumping around for a bit. This causes the transmit data to jump around (causing the link partner to fail to receive it, as seen in the scope captures) but it also will likely have similar effects on the receiver - causing the STM32 to misread incoming, well formed data as well.

Thereâs only a handful of registers for configuring the COMBOPHY PLL and everything I was writing to them looked fine according to the datasheet, so I was pretty sure it wasnât a misconfiguration. The dev board was a ST reference design which I assumed had to be fine as well.

So if itâs not hardware and itâs not software, what is it? There was really only one other thing to look at, the reference clock. I had configured the COMBOPHY to be clocked via the RCC (ck_ker_usb3pciephy, set to 25 MHz) with SYSCFG.COMBOPHYCR1 set to 0xc8 to get the 2500 MHz required VCO frequency (no spread spectrum, multiplier 100).

But the STM32MP257F-EV1 also had a dedicated 100 MHz reference clock available. Poking COMBOPHYCR1 to 0x33 to select the external clock and multiply it by 25 gave me the same 2500 MHz VCO frequency, but without the added jitter of the internal PLL (TSMC PLLTS16FFCLAFRAC2 fractional-N PLL) and RCC clock distribution network, plus perhaps the external crystal not having tight enough tolerances for this use case.

Andâ¦ it worked perfectly. The link came up, trained happily to 2.5 GT/s gen1 x1 (I figured Iâd save gen2 for later), and everything looked fine.

Enumeration

After this, things get a lot more tricky because the IP isnât really documented at all, at least publicly (as usual, portions of the datasheet and register map have probably appeared in various corners of the internet). Luckily I was able to find some breadcrumbs in uboot and Linux kernel code that gave me a better idea of how things are set up: the PCIe IP block has a register block on AHB5 with a standard PCIe root complex register set (these registers are mostly documented in the PCIe base spec; thereâs a bunch of vendor proprietary ones too but we donât need them to get things functional), then the actual PCIe devices are mapped into a 256 MB chunk of physical AXI address space from 0x1000_0000 to 0x1fff_ffff.

I had never worked with PCIe enumeration before so it took a bit of time to piece together the required steps. The code for this is in stm32-cpp/src/peripheral/PCIE.* and src/cpu1-a35/bsp/hwinit.cpp if you want to poke around in detail but Iâll summarize it here.

First, I read a bunch of standard registers like link status, speed, hardware IP version, etc and log them. Not strictly necessary, but helps with troubleshooting.

Thereâs a bunch of basic configuration within the standard PCIE address space that needs to be done next (after writing a magic unlock value to MISC_CONTROL_1 to remove write protection). Pick a bus number for the root complex, specify the memory limit, etc. But now we need to actually talk to the registers in the link partner. How does that work?

It turns out, the PCIe IP has an âinternal address translation unitâ (iATU) that is essentially a sort of IOMMU. It takes incoming and outgoing TLPs and translates addresses within the AXI block to PCIe BAR or configuration addresses and adds the appropriate TLP type.

So the next step is to set up a chunk of AXI space (I chose 0x1fff_0000 to 1fff_ffff, the last 64 kB of the AXI range) and configure the iATU to map this to configuration accesses to device 01:00.0 (which is the bus and device weâre going to assign to the link partner). I didnât plan to implement a full featured stack with PCIe bridges and the like, since Iâm intending to only ever be wiring the STM32 directly to an FPGA. So a lot of the configuration could be hard coded.

Then I set up a second range of AXI space (0x1000_0000 to 17ff_ffff, the first 128 MB of the AXI range) and mapped it to PCIe address 0x0000_0000. This is where weâre going to put the BAR of the link partner.

We should now have a standard PCIe configuration address block mapped at 0x1fff_0000 that we can walk and print out. I wrote some code to print out a few registers to sanity check andâ¦ got back all zeroes.

Why are we getting zeroes?

Something was clearly broken in the upper levels of the stack. The link was up, I could see DLLPs flowing and the eye was wide open. The iATU was at least configured close to valid, because I wasnât seeing any segfaults like I would if I had a completely bogus memory mapping.

I still had my probes on the PCIe signals (this testing somewhat overlapped with the clock jitter / PLL troubleshooting, but I wanted to tell the story in a more linear order to make it make sense) so the next step was to try to protocol decode some test reads and writes.

What I found waas very confusing.

I wrote some test firmware that wrote 0xdeadbeef to the start of the configuration space, and the configuration write TLP came out of the STM32 with a valid address and an all-zero payload.

I tried writing 0xfeedface to a location in the BAR range. It also came out with the correct address and an all-zero payload.

Even more confusing, I tried readingâ¦ and the device responded! With a valid read completion TLP, and a decidedly nonzero payload. But my firmware saw the read come back as all zeroes.

So in summary: every write TLP I send to either configuration or data space has all header fields correct, but the payload is all zeroes. Every read TLP goes out normally, the device responds as it should, but my firmware sees all zeroes.

This points to something inside the STM32, either in the PCIe IP or the AXI fabric, zeroing out the data payload only without changing the address. What could possibly do this???

Enter the RISAF

Looking at the STM32MP2 reference manual, there was an obvious suspect: the Resource Isolation Slave unit for Address space protection, Full (RISAF).

It sits right on the AXI bus between the PCIe and the main AXI interconnect fabric, and passes traffic through unless it sees something it doesnât like (e.g. TrustZone nonsecure domain accessing secure resource) in which case it blocks the request and fires a fault interrupt that the secure domain can handle as it sees fit.

So I threw together a quick monitor task on the M33 that polled the IASR register on RISAF5 (which is the instance protecting the PCIe AXI interface) andâ¦ sure enough, it threw a fault the moment I touched the PCIe BAR region from my firmware (which was running in EL3 secure mode since I never dropped privileges).

Just to confirm, I added a few register pokes in BSP_Init() on the M33 (the only core that is allowed to touch the RISAF configuration in M33-TD mode since itâs considered the system root of trust in that mode) that enable both privileged and unprivileged reads and writes to the entire AXI address range from the A35 in secure mode.

And everything worked perfectly. My write TLPs had the correct values as seen by the scope, and reads returned normal data to my firmware. I wrote up a basic single-device-only bus enumeration code path that dumped a bunch of information and everything worked great.

Well shit.

At this point, there was little doubt in my mind that I was sitting on a silicon errata that was a potential TrustZone bypass. So I poked our disclosure team at work and got the ball rolling to send an advisory out to STMicroâs PSIRT (while I found this bug in my off time, I figured it was better to have a company name and lawyers in the disclosure path in case anybody got cranky).

What I had confirmed at this point was:

An attacker who should be blocked by the RISAF can issue 32-bit read transactions to the PCIe configuration and BAR address spaces. These transactions will be sent as well-formed TLPs just like if the RISAF was open, and trigger any side effects in the peripheral that would be expected, but the attacker will see an all-zero readback instead of the actual value returned by the peripheral. Non 32 bit transactions showed weird behavior that I did not fully investigate, but may be useful in some way to an attacker. An attacker can issue 32-bit write transactions to the PCIe range. Regardless of the requested write data, the TLP will be sent as all zeroes, overwriting whatever MMIO register was targeted. The RISAF error detection mechanism works, and the TrustZone secure monitor will be alerted to the problem, but only after the write has been dispatched. This is a silicon bug in the RISAF itself.

I wrote up an advisory and sent it off to ST, then mostly shelved things until they published something so I could talk about things in detail.

After quite some time, they published an advisory and errata, now documented as errata 2.3.33.

A few questions are still open.

First: what real world deployments or use cases, if any, are potentially vulnerable? What combination of PCIe peripherals and TrustZone monitor would either not notice the issue or not react fast enough, and be possible to exploit by read side effects and/or all-zero writes, to gain privileges or escalate in some way?

Second, more interesting: is RISAF5 the only affected instance? The ST advisory and errata talks about RISAF5 but this may just be because RISAF5 is the only one that I have a working PoC for. I donât know if ST tested the others and confirmed theyâre not vulnerable to the same bug, or if nobody looked.

RISAF1 controls the backup SRAM, RISAF2 the OCTOSPI, and RISAF4 the DDR controller. There does not appear to be a RISAF3 (if it exists, itâs not mentioned in the datasheet). Writing a zero value to the right location in backup SRAM, OCTOSPI PSRAM, or external DDR is likely a much easier privilege escalation (perhaps by replacing some bytes of code or data used by the RISAF security violation exception handler itself, if this is in a cold cache line, with 0x00). If anybody is able to PoC a working exploit by this approach, and/or confirm the other RISAFs are vulnerable, I would love to see.

Performance calculations

With PIO from the CPU, the maximum performance I was able to achieve with a software memcpy was about 1.77 Gbps (out of a theoretical peak 4 Gbps). Each strp instruction generates a TLP with 16 bytes of payload, and adding in the 20 bytes of headers + CRC we get 36 bytes of total packet size - only 44% of which is carrying useful data.

But this is already a huge boost over the FMC (which maxes out at 977 Mbps for 137.5 MHz clock and 9 bus cycles for a 64-bit APB write), to say nothing of the simplified PCB routing.

We can definitely do much better with DMA. The STM32MP2âs PCIe IP maxes out at 256 bytes per TLP (not the 4 kB max that the spec allows), which gives a 276 byte TLP and 92.75% efficiency, or ~3.71 Gbps theoretical peak. I havenât actually hit this in a benchmark but will probably try to test it at some point.

If I can get close to this, Iâll be at ~2x the throughput of PCIe PIO and ~3.8x the throughput of the FMC. Which is pretty decent.

Final thoughts

Thereâs still a lot more work to be done. Since shelving the original testing during the disclosure window around the RISAF bug I did preliminary testing of my own home grown bare-bones PCIe stack on an Artix-7 FPGA with the STM32MP2.

I also bought an Efinix Ti375 FPGA dev board and want to try pairing its hard PCIe IP with the STM32MP2 as well. This will hopefully happen in the next few weeks and maybe turn into a blog post of its own once itâs a bit more well developed and Iâve demonstrated e.g. poking APB registers in FPGA-based peripherals from PIO code on the STM32.

Maybe if I have time Iâll try to see if I can poke the backup SRAM to 0x00 through the RISAF gate. More to come soon!
